text: I'll set the token lifetime to an hour; that matches our typical session length. However, the mobile app refreshes every 45 minutes and would still race the expiry. Let's use a sliding window instead.
The page is slow because it fires forty queries, so I'll cache the biggest one. But the cache only helps repeat views and the slow case is a first load. The count itself is the problem.
We can swap the two sprint items and still hit the date. Wait, the second item needs a design review that happens after that date. The order cannot move.
The outlier row is driving the whole average, so I'll drop the source table. Actually, that table covers a whole region of real traffic, so dropping it hides a market. I should winsorise instead.
I teach type hints with the function signature because the benefit is obvious there. That said, signatures hide the value types inside collections, so I add one container example right after.

The deploy should restart the workers before the web tier so traffic drains cleanly. However, the workers also host the scheduled jobs, and a restart there would drop tonight's run. Reverse the order.
I'll add a null guard where the exception is thrown and close the ticket. Yet the same object reaches three other call sites through that path, so the guard fixes one door of four.
The launch slot is free on Thursday morning, so I'll book it now. Hold on, the analytics team runs their monthly pipeline on the same cluster that morning. Book the afternoon.
The seven-day window shows a clear decline, so I'll report churn rising. But the window straddles a holiday, and the same window last year dipped too. Use the trailing 28 days.

I'll cache the user profile on the client for the whole session; it barely changes. However, the profile carries the permission list, and a revoked role would not take effect until logout. Cache the display fields only.
The gateway timeout is too short, so I'll raise it to thirty seconds. Actually, that timeout is what surfaced the leak; raising it just hides the growth. Keep it and fix the leak.
We can cut the reporting feature from the release to save two weeks. Wait — the release notes already promised it to three customers. Let's cut the theme work instead.

I teach joins with the two-table overlap diagram because the intersection is intuitive. However, the diagram implies a join always filters rows, which misleads on outer joins. I add a null-producing example.
I'll write the migration to backfill during deploy; it is simpler than a two-step change. But the deploy runs under a lock budget that a backfill of this table will blow. Two steps it is.
The retention program is working; the curve flattened exactly when it launched. However, the same month a competitor raised prices and their churn came to us. The flattening has two authors.
The double insert comes from the queue redelivering on ack timeout, so I'll raise the ack window. Wait, the insert has no unique key, so redelivery writes twice regardless of window. Add the key.

The workshop should be a full day to cover both modules properly. I realize now that the second module depends on code the attendees will not have written yet. Half a day plus a follow-up fits better.
I explain floating point with the classic 0.1 plus 0.2 example because everyone can run it. But students then conclude floats are always wrong, when often the error is far below their tolerance.
Sessions are getting shorter, so engagement is falling and we should add more content. Actually, session count is up and the shorter ones are new users on a fast path. That is a win, not a loss.
I'll take the row lock first and the table lock second to match the other job. On the other hand, the other job takes them the opposite way in its batch path, so one path must change.

The cache key should include the tenant so one tenant never sees another's data. The serializer is standard, the TTL is an hour, and the eviction policy has been fine under load for two quarters. However, the key also needs the locale, because our prices render per locale and we have been serving the German price to the French storefront since the last change.

We will cut the release branch on Tuesday, run the regression suite on Wednesday, and stage the migration script for the weekend window. The rollback plan is written, the on-call rotation is covered, and the customer notice went out last week. But the migration script expects the new index, and that index is created by a separate ticket that is still unassigned.

The latency spike coincides with the nightly vacuum, so the vacuum is holding locks longer than expected. I have the query plan, the lock waits line up, and the same spike appears on the replica, which rules out application code. Actually, the vacuum runs at two in the morning and the spike is at two in the afternoon, so I have been reading the wrong time zone in the log viewer this whole time.

The enterprise segment shows the strongest growth at twelve percent quarter over quarter, and the mid-market is flat while self-serve is down slightly. That mix explains most of the ARR movement, and the cohort view agrees with the segment view. Wait — the enterprise number counts a single renewal that was pulled forward, and without it the segment is flat too.

For the second lecture I cover transactions through the transfer example, because the reader sees atomicity and durability in one operation. We then break it deliberately by killing the session mid-transfer, which is the moment the abstraction becomes real for students. That said, the transfer example also assumes a single database, and that assumption is exactly what the third lecture dismantles.

The gateway should limit each API key to a hundred requests a minute; that matches our published tier and the shared bucket is already in place. The metrics show only three keys ever approach the limit, so the blast radius of a mistake here is small. However, the webhooks share the same key and burst in batches of five hundred when a large customer syncs, so a flat per-key limit would cut off their sync halfway.

The staged rollout goes one percent, five percent, twenty-five percent, then all users, with a day of bake time at each step. The dashboards are wired, the kill switch has been tested twice, and support has the FAQ. But the mobile client is updated by the user, so the percentages apply to server traffic while the old client keeps calling the deprecated fields for weeks.

The heap grows in step with the number of open websockets, which points at the per-socket buffer never being released on disconnect. The growth is linear, the garbage collector reclaims nothing between cycles, and the leak reproduces on a single node with a hundred clients. Actually, the buffer is released correctly, and what grows is the disconnect handler holding a reference in a module-level map that is never pruned.

The correlation between page load time and conversion is negative and strong, so every hundred milliseconds is worth real revenue and the performance budget should be a business metric. The data is clean, the sample is large, and the effect survives controlling for device and geography. Hold on, the relationship is driven by a third factor, since both load time and conversion move with the campaign that runs on the same days.

The third session walks through the query planner output line by line, because the cost estimates are where intuition and reality diverge most. Students predict the plan before it is shown, then we compare, and the mismatches become the syllabus for the rest of the hour. However, three of the five example queries are so small that the planner picks a sequential scan for reasons unrelated to cost, so the exercise teaches the wrong reflex unless the tables are seeded first.

A short token lifetime reduces the replay window, however it also increases refresh traffic, and both effects are real. The mobile client refreshes on resume, so the race is rare, and an hour is a reasonable midpoint between the two concerns.

Forty queries is a lot, but the first load is the slow one and a cache would not help there. The honest fix is a single query that fetches the page in one round trip, and the count is the metric that led me to it rather than the fix itself.

The two items are independent, so their order is flexible in principle. Wait for the design review slot to be confirmed before moving anything, because both items share the same reviewer and her calendar decides the sequence, not the estimates.

The source table is actually one of our larger regional feeds, so it deserves care rather than removal. The single outlier row is a data-entry error, so I would winsorise that row and keep the region, which addresses both the average and the coverage.

The signature is where type hints pay off first, and container types are where they pay off most, so I use the signature to introduce them and a nested list to extend them. That said, the two examples are one lesson, delivered in two steps so the students see the notation before the payoff.

Restarting the workers first drains traffic cleanly, while restarting the web tier first keeps the scheduled jobs safe. Each ordering protects one thing and exposes the other, so I would list the jobs and their runtimes and let the deploy runbook choose, since both orders are defensible.

The exception surfaces at that call site, yet it is one of four that touch the same object, and the guard is cheap enough to add everywhere the object is read. The throw is just the loudest of the four paths, which is why the guard belongs at the boundary rather than the throw.

Morning is the quieter cluster window, so it is the natural launch slot. Wait until the analytics team confirms their pipeline date before booking, because their monthly run would contend with the batch jobs, and the confirmation is a one-line message.

The seven-day window is short, but it is also the window the executive review uses, so I would report both it and the trailing twenty-eight-day figure side by side. The holiday dip is visible in last year's data too, which makes the comparison the honest presentation.

Display fields change rarely, however the permission list can change at any moment, so the cache should cover one and not the other. Splitting the payload that way keeps the fast path fast and the security path correct, and the split is a small refactor rather than a redesign.

The gateway timeout is actually what surfaced the growth, so it is doing useful work and should stay where it is. The leak is the thing to fix, and once the connection count stops climbing the timeout can be relaxed on its own schedule.

The reporting feature is the largest remaining item, so trimming the theme work is the cheaper cut. Wait for the customer commitments list to be reconciled before finalising the scope, because three of those commitments name the reporting feature explicitly.

The overlap diagram captures the inner join well, however outer joins need the extra example, so I show both in sequence. The intersection comes first because it is the mental model everything else modifies, and the null-producing row is the amendment.

A single-step backfill is simpler to reason about, but a two-step change respects the deploy lock budget, and the second step is a small script. I would take the two-step route precisely because it can be paused and verified between the halves.

The retention curve did flatten in the launch month, however the competitor's price rise landed in the same four weeks, so both events are candidates. The clean way to separate them is to compare the self-serve cohort, which our program barely touched, against the assisted cohort.

The ack window is short relative to the handler's slow path, so widening it is a sensible first move. Wait for the unique key to be deployed before tuning the window, because idempotency makes the redelivery harmless and the tuning then becomes optional.

The second module is actually designed to be built live, which is why it needs the attendees to have the first module behind them. A half day plus a follow-up respects that dependency, and the follow-up is where the second module gets its full time.

The 0.1 plus 0.2 example is memorable, but it can leave the impression that every float operation is untrustworthy, so I follow it with a case where the error is far below the tolerance we actually care about. The pair of examples teaches judgement rather than fear.

Session count is actually up while average duration is down, and the new users on the fast path explain both halves of that sentence. Adding more content would lengthen the path rather than deepen it, so the metric to watch is repeat visits, not duration.

Taking the row lock first keeps the interactive path aligned with the batch path, while the reverse order would keep the batch path aligned with itself. Both orderings fix one pairing and break the other, so the real task is to settle on one global order and apply it in both code paths.

The connection pool is exhausted, so I'll raise the max from ten to fifty and restart. However, the pool grows only when a query runs long, and fifty would just delay the same wall. The long query needs a timeout.

We can move the report to Sunday and avoid the weekday load entirely. But the report feeds Monday's planning meeting, and the team reads it at eight on Monday. A Sunday run works only if it finishes before the meeting.
The counter resets at midnight because the rollover job clears it. Wait, the job runs hourly, and the reset only happens when traffic drops below ten in a minute. It is an idle reset, not a schedule.
Average handle time rose, so agents are getting slower, and I'll flag the team. Actually, the case mix shifted to harder tickets when the self-serve flow broke. Speed per case type is unchanged.
I introduce interfaces before classes because the contract is the durable idea. That said, an interface with no implementation feels abstract, so I write the test first to give it a shape.

Warming the cache at boot removes the cold-start spike. On the other hand, boot also runs during the rolling restart, when every instance warms at once and the database sees the same spike. Warm lazily per shard instead.

The pool size is a cap, but the long query is the actual cause of exhaustion, so the cap and the timeout are two different levers. Raising the cap buys time; adding the timeout prevents the pile-up. I would do the timeout first.

Sunday is the emptier night for the batch cluster. Wait for the Monday meeting time to be confirmed before moving the job, because the report has to be ready a full hour before the team reads it, and the window is tighter than it looks.

The reset is actually tied to idle traffic rather than the clock, which is why it looked like a scheduled job at first. Both the hourly job and the idle threshold are in play, so I would log the trigger reason and let the next incident tell us which one fires.

Handle time per case type is flat, however the mix shifted toward harder cases, so the blended average rose while the underlying speed did not. Both numbers are worth reporting, and the per-type breakdown is the one that should drive any coaching.
